newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Moroccan king sets massive dam in motion.
newsitem.headline: Moroccan king sets massive dam in motion.

text.p: Standing atop a soaring dam, Moroccan King Hassan on Thursday set waters flowing from a massive reservoir to achieve an irrigation "dream of generations".
Accompanied by visiting Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro, whose country provided 34 percent of the financing for the $968 million project, the king said:
"By the end of 1997 with this dam we will achieve the irrigation of one million hectares (2.5 million acres). It is the dream of generations that became reality."
Watched by about 10,000 people from the Gharb region, King Hassan added: "This project was built for future generations and will guarantee jobs for 250,000 people."
Young girls in traditional red and green dresses strewed flower petals ahead of the king and his guest as they arrived for the ceremony.
As flags fluttered in a breeze, the king pressed a button to free water through the 80 metre (260 feet) dam to start irrigation.

The Al Wadha dam, Morocco's biggest, is 125 kms (78 miles) east of Rabat and, according to the public works ministry, has a capacity of 3.8 billion cubic metres. The project includes a hydroelectric power plant.

Finance Minister Mohamed Kabbaj told reporters the project's total cost was 9.0 billion dirhams ($957 million), of which 730 million dirhams was paid as compensation to 1,100 families evacuated from the site.
He said the reservoir would dramatically reduce damage caused in the area by floods, which cost the state about 200 million dirhams a year.
The dam will provide 16 percent of Morocco's hydroelectric power output. It will also transfer up to 700 million cubic metres of drinking water for Casablanca and southern areas of Rabat.
Water from the dam, which lies between three small hills, will also feed farmland of the Gharb region, with a population of 1.24 million people.
The area has five sugar refineries, four rice processing factories, seven flour meal plants, a crude oil refinery and 15 other units for farm products, cattle feed and packaging.

The sugar refineries represent 50 percent of Morocco's sugar output and experts said that in the future sugar production in the area will rise to 270,000 tonnes -- 195,000 tonnes of cane, the rest beet -- from 212,000 tonnes.

Morocco, which suffers from cyclical drought, has around 60 other large and medium dams. Public Works Minister Abdelaziz Meziane told a news conference on Tuesday: "This (Al Wadha) dam is the biggest dam Morocco has ever had, we will not be able to build another one of that importance in the future because of its exceptional site." ($1=9.4 dirhams)
